claims.text: The initial material is as-cast HfMoTaTiZr.
A portion of Hf and Ta should be substituted with Ti and Nb.
Substituting Hf and Ta with lighter elements such as Ti and Nb will reduce alloy density.
The proposed substitution can preserve a single-phase BCC microstructure.
Solid-solution strengthening in this alloy is driven by atomic-size and shear-modulus mismatch.
The high yield strength of HfMoTaTiZr is attributable to solid-solution strengthening.
Atomic-size and shear-modulus mismatch can be maintained after replacing some heavy elements with lighter elements.
Maintaining atomic-size and shear-modulus mismatch will maintain the solid-solution strengthening effect.
The modified alloy will have a lower density than as-cast HfMoTaTiZr.
The modified alloy will retain the room-temperature mechanical performance of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr.
The modified alloy will retain the high-temperature mechanical performance of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr through 1000 °C.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has a density of 10.21 g cm−3.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has a room-temperature yield strength of 1600 MPa.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has an elevated-temperature yield strength of 855 MPa.
Mechanical performance should be evaluated from room temperature to 1000 °C under uniaxial compression.
The modified alloy should be tested in compression at room temperature and 1000 °C while measuring yield strength and density.
The hypothesis is rejected if modified-alloy yield strength is below 90% of baseline at either room temperature or 1000 °C.
The consequences of the proposed substitution for strengthening and mechanical properties are uncertain.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis promises no sacrifice in mechanical performance, but the rejection rule permits yield strength to fall by as much as 10% without falsification.

The 855 MPa baseline is labeled only as an elevated-temperature value, while the rejection rule implicitly treats a baseline at 1000 °C as available; the hypothesis does not explicitly associate 855 MPa with 1000 °C.
